trait_value_raw: The Tetratheca species are buzz pollinated
source_section: Abstract, p.248; Introduction, p.249; Table 2, p.251
notes: AusTraits vocabulary has no dedicated 'buzz' pollination term; mapped to the generic 'bee' vector under pollination_vector_known (not pollination_syndrome) because the evidence is direct field observation, not floral-morphology inference: bees were seen visiting flowers and sonicating/vibrating the anthers, and captured bees (Table 2) carried predominantly Tetratheca pollen. Bees identified carrying predominantly Tetratheca pollen were species of Lasioglossum (subgenus Chilalictus), plus one Megachile hackeriapis (Table 2, T. paynterae subsp. paynterae only)

trait_value_raw: The Tetratheca species are buzz pollinated
notes: AusTraits vocabulary has no dedicated 'buzz' pollination term; mapped to the generic 'bee' vector under pollination_vector_known (not pollination_syndrome). The direct observation/pollen-load evidence (Table 2, p.251) is specifically for T. paynterae subsp. paynterae only; for this taxon the 'buzz pollinated' claim rests on the Abstract/Introduction's general statement plus the Methods (p.250) generalisation that floral morphology and bee behaviour at flowers are similar for the four taxa, not on taxon-specific field data.

source_section: Methods, Study species and area, p.250
notes: Not individually described for this taxon; generalised from the T. paynterae subsp. paynterae description on the strength of the Methods statement that 'floral morphology and bee behaviour at flowers are similar for the four taxa' (p.250). Poricidal anther dehiscence is also the mechanism underlying the buzz-pollination trait proposed separately (see the 'buzz_pollination' candidate-trait rows) — the two are closely related aspects of the same pollen-release mechanism.
